title: Ibn Arabi
hookLine: the mystic born in Murcia, who traveled east to Damascus

cards: Yesterday's philosopher asks to meet a boy. The boy, in his own later telling, is barely grown, and people have been talking about him.
Ibn Rushd rises to greet him and asks, more or less: is what you have found by inner opening the same as what we find by reasoning? The boy says yes. Ibn Rushd looks pleased.
Then the boy says no. And between that yes and that no, the boy reports, the old philosopher went pale. The boy was Ibn Arabi, and the story is his own.

teach.b: Ibn Arabi was born in Murcia, in al-Andalus, and never really stopped traveling.
He went east, to Mecca, where he began a vast book called The Meccan Openings, and on through the cities of the Muslim world until he settled in Damascus, where he is buried.
People called him al-Shaykh al-Akbar: the greatest master. Begin with a verse he and other Sufis return to.
In Pickthall's translation: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance."

In his reading, if God's face is wherever you turn, then the world is full of signs, and every moment can be a meeting. Elsewhere the Qur'an says of each person, "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein."

teach.h: A KNOWING THAT IS OPENED, NOT PROVED.
teach.b: For Ibn Arabi, knowing that nearness is not a conclusion you reason your way to. It is opened in you, the inner opening behind his no to Ibn Rushd.
Reason goes far, in his view, but there is a kind of knowing it can't hand you. Now the honest part. His books are dense and daring, and Muslims have read them in sharply different ways.
Among his Sufi readers he is treasured.

teach.h: REVERED BY SOME, ATTACKED BY OTHERS.
teach.b: Some scholars, Ibn Taymiyya among them, attacked parts of his teaching as error. Others defended him as a master misunderstood. That argument is still going, so today's line comes with two words attached on purpose.

how: Some Sufi orders study Ibn Arabi's works closely and visit his tomb in Damascus; other Muslim scholars have criticized parts of his teaching, and the debate over him continues.

games.q: you're young, and Ibn Rushd, the great philosopher, asks you: is what you've found by inner opening the same as what we find by reason? what do you say?
o: no, they have nothing to do with each other.
games.why: he says yes, and then no. in his telling, reason goes far, but there's a knowing it can't hand you, and the philosopher went pale.

practice: Choose one thing you can't explain and don't need to solve right now: why you're here at all, where someone you lost has gone.
Let it sit beside you without cracking it, the way Ibn Arabi let his yes and his no sit side by side, and when your thoughts start building an answer, set it down and come back to the question.
If you pray, bring the mystery into your prayer; if you don't, just keep it company.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Arabi. The mystic from Murcia who traveled to Damascus, called the greatest master by those who love him, and argued over by those who don't. Today's word.
